claims.text: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy undergoes extensive primary non-eutectic crystallization during solidification.
The undoped alloy crystallizes extensively under both rapid and slower cooling.
The undoped alloy exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence during reheating.
Approximately 2 at.% boron should be added to the base alloy.
Boron addition will increase chemical complexity and atomic-scale packing frustration.
Boron-induced packing frustration will perturb formation of the primary crystalline phases.
Boron is a potent glass-forming element.
Boron will increase local topological and chemical disorder in this alloy.
Boron will lower atomic mobility in this alloy.
The reduced mobility and increased disorder will suppress heterogeneous nucleation and growth of non-eutectic crystalline phases during cooling.
The boron-induced structural changes will widen the supercooled-liquid region during reheating.
The boron-modified alloy will retain more amorphous material than the undoped alloy during rapid and slower cooling.
The boron-modified alloy will exhibit fewer and/or delayed DSC crystallization exotherms.
Boron addition will raise the onset temperature for primary crystallization on reheating.
Boron addition will increase the critical cooling rate required for vitrification.
The predicted improvement is expected at cooling rates above approximately 10^5 K/s.
The predicted improvement is expected during reheating restricted to at least 10–20 °C below the original crystallization-onset temperature.
At significantly lower cooling rates or under unoptimized reheating schedules, boron may not improve amorphous retention.
Boron has enhanced glass formation in other similar alloy systems.
Interactions between boron and phosphorus may alter the effectiveness of boron in this specific alloy.

contradictions.description: Enhanced glass-forming ability and retention at slower cooling imply that vitrification should be possible at a lower critical cooling rate, whereas the predicted outcome states that the critical cooling rate will increase.

The hypothesis broadly predicts improvement during both rapid and slower cooling, but the only numerical domain supplied is above approximately 10^5 K/s, while significantly lower rates are excluded; the claimed slower-cooling regime is therefore undefined.

The hypothesis predicts and proposes testing a 10–20 °C increase in crystallization onset, but the boundary says reheating should remain 10–20 °C below the original onset. If that is a maximum reheating temperature, the scan cannot observe either the original or the predicted higher onset.
